title: Forgiving
hookLine: a grudge that won't leave, and the five ways to remove it (AN 5.161)
tomorrow: how do you guard a door that fits in your pocket?

lines: THEY SAID SORRY. IT STILL PLAYS.
cards: They apologized. You said it's fine. And still, at odd moments, in the shower or on the walk home, the old scene plays again.
A grudge is a guest that won't take the hint. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha gives five ways to remove one. Four sound like what you'd expect from a teacher of kindness.
The fifth sounds strange at first: simply stop paying attention to the person. So which of the five is the oddest, and which one fits your grudge?

teach.b: Here are the five. Toward the one you hold a grudge against, grow loving-kindness. Or grow compassion.
Or grow equanimity, an even mind.
Or stop giving them your attention: don't feed the scene, let it go quiet.

Or remember that they own their actions; what they did is theirs to carry, not yours. The odd one, not paying attention, turns out to be the plainest. A grudge lives on replays, and this one just stops buying tickets.
And the last way isn't a curse on them. It's a release for you: their actions follow them, so you can set the heavy bag down and walk on lighter.
Now this week, all of it, one line at a time. Loneliness: the elephant's forest, then the walk back: alone, then together. Neighbors: the Metta Sutta names the near: next door.
Community: the Vajjis kept meeting: meet in harmony. Strangers: the tired man on the bus: they have a whole life.
Anger at home: Vedehika and the saw: pause. The small stuff: only one arrow. Put them together and they're a way of living with people, near and far.
Forgiving is the one that keeps the rest possible.

how: Buddhists work with grudges through loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity practice; some teachers also point to AN 5.161's quieter ways: not dwelling on the person, and reflecting that each owns their actions.

o: pretending a wrong never happened, to keep the peace
waiting until the other person has earned it back
removing a grudge, by one of five ways the Buddha taught

games.q: five ways to remove a grudge — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha's only way to remove a grudge is to feel loving-kindness
AN 5.161 gives five, including simply not paying attention to the person.
one of the five ways is to remember that people own their actions
what they did is theirs to carry; you don't have to carry it for them.

games.q: a coworker took credit for your idea months ago, apologized, and you still replay it every time they talk in meetings. which of the five fits best?
o: not paying attention: stop replaying the scene when they speak.
keep the grudge as protection, so it can't happen again.
pretend to like them more than you do, until the feeling fades.
games.why: when the grudge lives on replays, the plainest of the five fits: stop feeding the scene. the other four are still there if you need them.

practice: Bring to mind one small grudge, not the biggest one you carry.

Choose one of the five, whichever feels possible today: a kind wish for them, compassion for whatever made them do it, an even mind, simply letting the scene go quiet, or the thought, that's theirs to carry.
Stay with that one way for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving: in the Anguttara Nikaya, five ways to remove a grudge, from loving-kindness to letting the scene go quiet.

orig.note: Pali: a grudge, resentment; the thing AN 5.161 teaches how to remove.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: let it go, one of five ways at a time. Three of nine, a full week behind you.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.161 (Aghatapativinaya Sutta: five ways of removing resentment: loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, non-attention, and reflecting that the person is owner of their actions)
